In 1913 income per head in Latvia and Estonia stood at the level of Finland or Italy, and even agrarian Lithuania was richer than Greece or Portugal \parencite[129--30]{norkus_2023_output}. When Red Army soldiers entered the Baltic republics under the mutual-assistance pacts of 1939 they wrote home in astonishment: `the store is full of all sorts of fabrics, whatever the soul desires, and there is not a single person, not to mention a line' \parencite[279]{meltyukhov2014en}. By 1990, after forty-five years inside the Soviet Union, income per head in the three republics was about half that of Finland and three-fifths that of the Western periphery; by 2024, after three decades of reform, European Union membership and `Baltic tiger' growth, they remained in Europe's periphery, and the richest of them in 1913, Latvia, had become the poorest \parencite[93]{koll_2025_reinterpretation}. Three small, literate, egalitarian economies, which possessed from the outset much of what the catch-up literature regards as the social capability needed to grow \parencite[388]{abramovitz1986}, have failed over 110 years and under three economic regimes to leave the periphery into which the nineteenth century placed them. The gap has begun to close. Following % ============================================================= % ESTIMATING LATVIAN GDP, 1937-1995 % ============================================================= \section{Estimating Latvian GDP, 1937--1995} \label{sec:method} \subsection{The output approach and the reliability of Soviet statistics} For the Soviet period only the production side of national income can be reconstructed. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The two diverge widely: the official Soviet index of Latvian industrial output at constant prices rises between 1940 and 1990 by several times the increase recorded by the physical-product index compiled here (Table~\ref{tab:sectoral}). The official index also values its 1940 base at an arbitrary lat--rouble parity that undervalued the last pre-Soviet year several-fold (Misiunas and Taagepera suspected in addition that only the five months of Soviet rule were counted; Mertelsmann finds for Estonia that the whole year was); its claim that industry had surpassed 1940 by 1947 is contradicted by the physical series \parencites[109]{years_of_dependence}[167]{mertelsmann_2003_there}[234]{krumins_2017_sovetizacijas}. The indices below rest almost entirely on physical quantities, on employment and on inputs; the one place where value data at comparable prices enter, trade turnover, is flagged and its bias bounded in the sensitivity analysis. \subsection{The 1990 benchmark} The Soviet-period series is anchored to Bolotin's estimate of the GDP of the Latvian SSR in 1990, the first systematic attempt to express the accounts of all fifteen republics in international dollars \parencite[181--92]{bolotin1992}. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The two diverge widely: the official Soviet index of Latvian industrial output at constant prices rises between 1940 and 1990 by several times the increase recorded by the physical-product index compiled here (Table~\ref{tab:sectoral}). The official index also values its 1940 base at an arbitrary lat--rouble parity that undervalued the last pre-Soviet year several-fold (Misiunas and Taagepera suspected in addition that only the five months of Soviet rule were counted; Mertelsmann finds for Estonia that the whole year was); its claim that industry had surpassed 1940 by 1947 is contradicted by the physical series \parencites[109]{years_of_dependence}[167]{mertelsmann_2003_there}[234]{krumins_2017_sovetizacijas}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The two diverge widely: the official Soviet index of Latvian industrial output at constant prices rises between 1940 and 1990 by several times the increase recorded by the physical-product index compiled here (Table~\ref{tab:sectoral}). The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The two diverge widely: the official Soviet index of Latvian industrial output at constant prices rises between 1940 and 1990 by several times the increase recorded by the physical-product index compiled here (Table~\ref{tab:sectoral}). The official index also values its 1940 base at an arbitrary lat--rouble parity that undervalued the last pre-Soviet year several-fold (Misiunas and Taagepera suspected in addition that only the five months of Soviet rule were counted; Mertelsmann finds for Estonia that the whole year was); its claim that industry had surpassed 1940 by 1947 is contradicted by the physical series \parencites[109]{years_of_dependence}[167]{mertelsmann_2003_there}[234]{krumins_2017_sovetizacijas}. The indices below rest almost entirely on physical quantities, on employment and on inputs; the one place where value data at comparable prices enter, trade turnover, is flagged and its bias bounded in the sensitivity analysis. \subsection{The 1990 benchmark} The Soviet-period series is anchored to Bolotin's estimate of the GDP of the Latvian SSR in 1990, the first systematic attempt to express the accounts of all fifteen republics in international dollars \parencite[181--92]{bolotin1992}. The parities, by sector of origin, were 0.40 dollars per rouble in agriculture, 1.80 in industry, 1.10 in construction, 2.80 in transport, 1.45 in trade and 3.30 in other services, or 1.82 for GDP as a whole \parencite[181, 184]{bolotin1992}. For Latvia the result is \lv{1990}~\intlnineteen{} per head, between Lithuania's 7,475 and Estonia's 8,425. Table~\ref{tab:benchmarks} shows the sectoral composition in roubles, with services other than trade and transport allocated by the 1987 Soviet input--output table \parencite{wbinputoutput1987}, beside the 1935 benchmark of \textcite{norkuslatvia1935} on which the interwar series rests. The rouble shares are domestic-price weights, like the lats shares of 1935, and are the weights with which the volume indices are combined; the dollar conversion applies to the total alone. They are at the market prices of 1990, so that product taxes and subsidies are carried within the sectors that bore them; no re-pricing to adjusted factor cost was attempted, since no republican data on the incidence of net product taxes by branch exist, and the only socialist economies for which the World Bank reports the ratio of product taxes less subsidies to value-added, Bulgaria and Ukraine in 1980--90, show about 0.5 per cent \parencite{wdi2024}.\footnote{The turnover tax, the principal product tax, was levied on final consumption goods and accrued to the republic where the finished good was made, as with cotton fabric woven in the Baltics from cheaply procured Uzbek cotton \parencite[20]{yasin_1993_economic}.} \input{../../Tables/latvia/T1_benchmarks.tex} Three features of the benchmark need stating, because the reconstruction stands or falls with it. First, its level is conservative. Bolotin's figure for the Soviet Union as a whole, 6,275~\intlnineteen{} per head, lies below Maddison's own estimate for 1987, and the bilateral Austria--USSR comparison on which it draws placed the Union at 32 per cent of the United States where the CIA had placed it at 42 per cent \parencite[318--19]{Maddison1998b}. Maddison nevertheless built the Maddison Project's 1990 levels for the republics from Bolotin's republic-to-Union ratios of 1991 rather than 1990, ratios inflated by the first year of transition, and then carried them backwards with net material product growth \parencite[181--2]{maddisonworldeconomy}; the consequences for Latvia are shown in Table~\ref{tab:previous} below. Second, the parities are Union-wide, so that the conversion assumes that relative prices in Latvia were those of the Soviet Union as a whole. For the material sectors this is a reasonable approximation in a planned economy with administered prices; for services, where the parity of 3.30 dollars per rouble reflects the very low rouble wages of the non-market sector, it is less certain, and the resulting share of services in Latvian GDP at rouble prices, 47 per cent, is above the 34 per cent implied by the World Bank's 1990 sectoral data \parencite{wbstatisticalhandbook1994}; the sensitivity of the series to this allocation is examined below. Third, there is no alternative.\footnote{Earlier claims ranged widely: PlanEcon's CIA-based estimate for Estonia in 1989 was 6,240 dollars against 5,000 for the Union \parencite[166]{kukk2005}.} Ponomarenko's accounts cover Russia alone and make no dollar conversion; the World Bank's GDP levels for 1980--91 were discontinued; the UNECE's `real GDP' indices for 1980--90 were taken from net material product, and the early Total Economy Database reproduced them \parencites{wbtransitionlatv}[32--3]{worldtables1995}[249]{UNECE1995}; the CIA's 1982 benchmark cannot be decomposed by republic, and the 1987 input--output table understates services too severely to serve as a benchmark \parencite[66--89]{wbinputoutput1987}. The practical reason is that 1990 is the only year for which republican accounts on an SNA definition and purchasing-power parities exist together. The test is demanding. The two series share no sources, the one resting on the republic's own statistics and the other on Soviet yearbooks and post-war archives; no weights, one using the structure of 1935 and the other that of 1990; and no benchmark, one a bilateral price comparison with Sweden, the other a purchasing-power-parity study of the Soviet republics fifty-five years later. That the Soviet-period series, extrapolated backwards over half a century of war, collectivisation and forced industrialisation, arrives within 3.5 per cent of an independently measured level in every year, and within 2 per cent in three of the four, is the strongest evidence available that the net error of the extrapolation is small. The population of the Abrene district at its transfer in 1944 is not counted in the sources available to us: King speaks only of `several thousands' of Latvian citizens, and Misiunas and Taagepera, like Hiden and Salmon, of about 2 per cent of the pre-war population % ============================================================= % ESTIMATING LATVIAN GDP, 1937-1995 % ============================================================= \section{Estimating Latvian GDP, 1937--1995} \label{sec:method} \subsection{The output approach and the reliability of Soviet statistics} For the Soviet period only the production side of national income can be reconstructed. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The two diverge widely: the official Soviet index of Latvian industrial output at constant prices rises between 1940 and 1990 by several times the increase recorded by the physical-product index compiled here (Table~\ref{tab:sectoral}). The official index also values its 1940 base at an arbitrary lat--rouble parity that undervalued the last pre-Soviet year several-fold (Misiunas and Taagepera suspected in addition that only the five months of Soviet rule were counted; Mertelsmann finds for Estonia that the whole year was); its claim that industry had surpassed 1940 by 1947 is contradicted by the physical series \parencites[109]{years_of_dependence}[167]{mertelsmann_2003_there}[234]{krumins_2017_sovetizacijas}. The indices below rest almost entirely on physical quantities, on employment and on inputs; the one place where value data at comparable prices enter, trade turnover, is flagged and its bias bounded in the sensitivity analysis. \subsection{The 1990 benchmark} The Soviet-period series is anchored to Bolotin's estimate of the GDP of the Latvian SSR in 1990, the first systematic attempt to express the accounts of all fifteen republics in international dollars \parencite[181--92]{bolotin1992}. The parities, by sector of origin, were 0.40 dollars per rouble in agriculture, 1.80 in industry, 1.10 in construction, 2.80 in transport, 1.45 in trade and 3.30 in other services, or 1.82 for GDP as a whole \parencite[181, 184]{bolotin1992}. For Latvia the result is \lv{1990}~\intlnineteen{} per head, between Lithuania's 7,475 and Estonia's 8,425. Table~\ref{tab:benchmarks} shows the sectoral composition in roubles, with services other than trade and transport allocated by the 1987 Soviet input--output table \parencite{wbinputoutput1987}, beside the 1935 benchmark of \textcite{norkuslatvia1935} on which the interwar series rests. The rouble shares are domestic-price weights, like the lats shares of 1935, and are the weights with which the volume indices are combined; the dollar conversion applies to the total alone. They are at the market prices of 1990, so that product taxes and subsidies are carried within the sectors that bore them; no re-pricing to adjusted factor cost was attempted, since no republican data on the incidence of net product taxes by branch exist, and the only socialist economies for which the World Bank reports the ratio of product taxes less subsidies to value-added, Bulgaria and Ukraine in 1980--90, show about 0.5 per cent \parencite{wdi2024}.\footnote{The turnover tax, the principal product tax, was levied on final consumption goods and accrued to the republic where the finished good was made, as with cotton fabric woven in the Baltics from cheaply procured Uzbek cotton \parencite[20]{yasin_1993_economic}.} \input{../../Tables/latvia/T1_benchmarks.tex} Three features of the benchmark need stating, because the reconstruction stands or falls with it. First, its level is conservative. Bolotin's figure for the Soviet Union as a whole, 6,275~\intlnineteen{} per head, lies below Maddison's own estimate for 1987, and the bilateral Austria--USSR comparison on which it draws placed the Union at 32 per cent of the United States where the CIA had placed it at 42 per cent \parencite[318--19]{Maddison1998b}. Maddison nevertheless built the Maddison Project's 1990 levels for the republics from Bolotin's republic-to-Union ratios of 1991 rather than 1990, ratios inflated by the first year of transition, and then carried them backwards with net material product growth \parencite[181--2]{maddisonworldeconomy}; the consequences for Latvia are shown in Table~\ref{tab:previous} below. Second, the parities are Union-wide, so that the conversion assumes that relative prices in Latvia were those of the Soviet Union as a whole. For the material sectors this is a reasonable approximation in a planned economy with administered prices; for services, where the parity of 3.30 dollars per rouble reflects the very low rouble wages of the non-market sector, it is less certain, and the resulting share of services in Latvian GDP at rouble prices, 47 per cent, is above the 34 per cent implied by the World Bank's 1990 sectoral data \parencite{wbstatisticalhandbook1994}; the sensitivity of the series to this allocation is examined below. Third, there is no alternative.\footnote{Earlier claims ranged widely: PlanEcon's CIA-based estimate for Estonia in 1989 was 6,240 dollars against 5,000 for the Union \parencite[166]{kukk2005}.} Ponomarenko's accounts cover Russia alone and make no dollar conversion; the World Bank's GDP levels for 1980--91 were discontinued; the UNECE's `real GDP' indices for 1980--90 were taken from net material product, and the early Total Economy Database reproduced them \parencites{wbtransitionlatv}[32--3]{worldtables1995}[249]{UNECE1995}; the CIA's 1982 benchmark cannot be decomposed by republic, and the 1987 input--output table understates services too severely to serve as a benchmark \parencite[66--89]{wbinputoutput1987}. The choice of 1990 means that the series is extrapolated backwards for more than fifty years from end-of-period weights. The practical reason is that 1990 is the only year for which republican accounts on an SNA definition and purchasing-power parities exist together. Two further considerations favour it: the reporting of 1989--90, at the height of glasnost, was more transparent than that of any earlier Soviet year, the manipulation of earlier returns having been publicly acknowledged by Baltic statisticians in 1988 \parencite{adlys1988}; and 1990 is a year in which the branches that barely existed in 1940, electrical engineering, chemicals, pharmaceuticals or microbus production, can be observed and weighted at all \parencites[278]{krumins_2017_tautsaimnieciba_1950}[303, 305]{krumins_2017_tautsaimnieciba_1960}. The cost is that half a century is valued at end-period relative prices, which, as the sensitivity analysis explains, tends to understate growth; the short answer is that the consequence can be tested directly, because the Soviet-period series meets an independent series with 1935 weights in 1937--40. \subsection{Volume indices and their sources} Table~\ref{tab:sources} summarises the indicators and sources for each sector; the online appendix documents every series year by year. The two series are spliced at 1940 by taking the average of the two estimates for that year, which moves the 1940 figure by less than half a per cent. The second overlap validates the benchmark. In 1990 the Soviet-period series stands 2.9 per cent below the modern series and in 1991 \ovd{1991} per cent above it: Bolotin's purchasing-power parities and the Maddison Project's 2011 ICP round, carried backwards with the national accounts, are two routes that share no data and arrive at the same level within 3 per cent. The series are spliced at 1991, the year of restored independence, by averaging. Thereafter the gap widens to \ovd{1992} per cent in 1992 before narrowing to \ovd{1995} per cent by 1995, because the Soviet-period series continues to value the collapse of Soviet-era output at 1990 weights and misses the new activities, above all in services, that were emerging unrecorded \parencite[260]{kyn_1997_eastern}, while the modern series, like Hamilton and de Vries's recent extrapolation of the post-Soviet republics from mid-1990s benchmarks, carries the weights of the surviving branches backwards and records a shallower decline \parencites[11]{imf_transition}[17]{hamilton_transition}. The first is the index-number problem of a single late benchmark. A late base assigns to each sector the relative prices of the end of the period, and since the sectors that grew fastest were those whose relative prices fell, late weights understate growth; this is the effect that Gerschenkron showed for Soviet machinery, when Bergson's GNP for 1928--37 grows by 175 per cent at 1928 prices and by 62 per cent at 1937 prices \parencites[453]{gerschenkron1957}[517]{feinsteinthomas2002}. It is far smaller here. The effect is concentrated in the early phases of industrialisation \parencite[85]{jonassardy1970}, and for the post-war Soviet economy it is modest: the CIA's move from 1970 to 1982 prices lowered measured growth over 1951--84 by about half a point a year \parencites[8]{cia1990}[156]{harrison1993}. The bound comes from the data: if 1990 weights understated Latvian growth over 1940--90, the Soviet-period series would arrive in 1937--40 systematically above the 1935-weighted interwar series, and it does not. And the procedure is that of every comparable reconstruction, the CIA's 1982 weights for 1950--90 among them, in which Maddison found `nothing untoward' \parencite[312]{Maddison1998b}. The second is the fixed ratio of value-added to gross output. Thomas and Feinstein's simulations found that the procedure understated value-added growth by between 0.15 and 1 percentage point a year; the Swedish accounts, which allow single- and double-deflated series to be compared, show an understatement of the deflator of 17 per cent over the three-quarters of a century after 1875 \parencites[19]{swedengdp_15602010}[148--53]{lobellschonkrantz2008}, and the bound in Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}, 14 per cent over the half-century, is in the lower part of that range, as befits indices that track output product by product and an economy that adhered to mass-production methods throughout its existence \parencite[195--7]{berend_centraleastern19441993}. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The two diverge widely: the official Soviet index of Latvian industrial output at constant prices rises between 1940 and 1990 by several times the increase recorded by the physical-product index compiled here (Table~\ref{tab:sectoral}). The official index also values its 1940 base at an arbitrary lat--rouble parity that undervalued the last pre-Soviet year several-fold (Misiunas and Taagepera suspected in addition that only the five months of Soviet rule were counted; Mertelsmann finds for Estonia that the whole year was); its claim that industry had surpassed 1940 by 1947 is contradicted by the physical series \parencites[109]{years_of_dependence}[167]{mertelsmann_2003_there}[234]{krumins_2017_sovetizacijas}. The indices below rest almost entirely on physical quantities, on employment and on inputs; the one place where value data at comparable prices enter, trade turnover, is flagged and its bias bounded in the sensitivity analysis. \subsection{The 1990 benchmark} The Soviet-period series is anchored to Bolotin's estimate of the GDP of the Latvian SSR in 1990, the first systematic attempt to express the accounts of all fifteen republics in international dollars \parencite[181--92]{bolotin1992}. Bolotin started from the republican GDP totals for 1990 compiled by Goskomstat in 1990--1, 1990 being one of the first years for which republican accounts on an SNA-type definition were compiled \parencite[43--4]{gulans_2015_rupnieciba} and the first with purchasing-power parities, and converted them into dollars with parities estimated, as he put it, `in practically full conformity' with the International Comparison Project. The parities, by sector of origin, were 0.40 dollars per rouble in agriculture, 1.80 in industry, 1.10 in construction, 2.80 in transport, 1.45 in trade and 3.30 in other services, or 1.82 for GDP as a whole \parencite[181, 184]{bolotin1992}. For Latvia the result is \lv{1990}~\intlnineteen{} per head, between Lithuania's 7,475 and Estonia's 8,425. Table~\ref{tab:benchmarks} shows the sectoral composition in roubles, with services other than trade and transport allocated by the 1987 Soviet input--output table \parencite{wbinputoutput1987}, beside the 1935 benchmark of \textcite{norkuslatvia1935} on which the interwar series rests. The rouble shares are domestic-price weights, like the lats shares of 1935, and are the weights with which the volume indices are combined; the dollar conversion applies to the total alone. They are at the market prices of 1990, so that product taxes and subsidies are carried within the sectors that bore them; no re-pricing to adjusted factor cost was attempted, since no republican data on the incidence of net product taxes by branch exist, and the only socialist economies for which the World Bank reports the ratio of product taxes less subsidies to value-added, Bulgaria and Ukraine in 1980--90, show about 0.5 per cent \parencite{wdi2024}.\footnote{The turnover tax, the principal product tax, was levied on final consumption goods and accrued to the republic where the finished good was made, as with cotton fabric woven in the Baltics from cheaply procured Uzbek cotton \parencite[20]{yasin_1993_economic}.} \input{../../Tables/latvia/T1_benchmarks.tex} Three features of the benchmark need stating, because the reconstruction stands or falls with it. First, its level is conservative. Bolotin's figure for the Soviet Union as a whole, 6,275~\intlnineteen{} per head, lies below Maddison's own estimate for 1987, and the bilateral Austria--USSR comparison on which it draws placed the Union at 32 per cent of the United States where the CIA had placed it at 42 per cent \parencite[318--19]{Maddison1998b}. Maddison nevertheless built the Maddison Project's 1990 levels for the republics from Bolotin's republic-to-Union ratios of 1991 rather than 1990, ratios inflated by the first year of transition, and then carried them backwards with net material product growth \parencite[181--2]{maddisonworldeconomy}; the consequences for Latvia are shown in Table~\ref{tab:previous} below. Second, the parities are Union-wide, so that the conversion assumes that relative prices in Latvia were those of the Soviet Union as a whole. For the material sectors this is a reasonable approximation in a planned economy with administered prices; for services, where the parity of 3.30 dollars per rouble reflects the very low rouble wages of the non-market sector, it is less certain, and the resulting share of services in Latvian GDP at rouble prices, 47 per cent, is above the 34 per cent implied by the World Bank's 1990 sectoral data \parencite{wbstatisticalhandbook1994}; the sensitivity of the series to this allocation is examined below. Third, there is no alternative.\footnote{Earlier claims ranged widely: PlanEcon's CIA-based estimate for Estonia in 1989 was 6,240 dollars against 5,000 for the Union \parencite[166]{kukk2005}.} Ponomarenko's accounts cover Russia alone and make no dollar conversion; the World Bank's GDP levels for 1980--91 were discontinued; the UNECE's `real GDP' indices for 1980--90 were taken from net material product, and the early Total Economy Database reproduced them \parencites{wbtransitionlatv}[32--3]{worldtables1995}[249]{UNECE1995}; the CIA's 1982 benchmark cannot be decomposed by republic, and the 1987 input--output table understates services too severely to serve as a benchmark \parencite[66--89]{wbinputoutput1987}. The choice of 1990 means that the series is extrapolated backwards for more than fifty years from end-of-period weights. The practical reason is that 1990 is the only year for which republican accounts on an SNA definition and purchasing-power parities exist together. Two further considerations favour it: the reporting of 1989--90, at the height of glasnost, was more transparent than that of any earlier Soviet year, the manipulation of earlier returns having been publicly acknowledged by Baltic statisticians in 1988 \parencite{adlys1988}; and 1990 is a year in which the branches that barely existed in 1940, electrical engineering, chemicals, pharmaceuticals or microbus production, can be observed and weighted at all \parencites[278]{krumins_2017_tautsaimnieciba_1950}[303, 305]{krumins_2017_tautsaimnieciba_1960}. The cost is that half a century is valued at end-period relative prices, which, as the sensitivity analysis explains, tends to understate growth; the short answer is that the consequence can be tested directly, because the Soviet-period series meets an independent series with 1935 weights in 1937--40. \subsection{Volume indices and their sources} Table~\ref{tab:sources} summarises the indicators and sources for each sector; the online appendix documents every series year by year. First, archival material is used to fill the early post-war years that the yearbooks cover incompletely, not merely to decorate the series; but, unlike for Lithuania and Estonia, no archival compilation of late-1980s output values at the product level could be found for Latvia, so that the 129 product series are consolidated into 22 minor branches by averaging and the minor branches weighted with the 1987 input--output study and the World Bank's 1993 valuation \parencites[82--5]{wbinputoutput1987}[289]{wbtransitionlatv}. Second, the series cover the civilian economy as reported to the republican statistical office. Gerschenkron's late industrialiser borrows technology rather than inventing it and substitutes banks or the state for the prerequisites it lacks, and Solow's model predicts faster growth where capital per worker is scarce; Lewis's surplus labour raises average productivity as it moves off the land; and the cumulative effect of all three widens markets and permits scale economies \parencites[8]{gerschenkron1962}[70--1]{solow1956}{lewis1954}[22]{abramovitz_david1996}. The Baltic states are an unusually clean test of these propositions. The human-capital component of their social capability, literacy and schooling, was high throughout, by the standards of the European periphery \parencite[71]{raun_2017_literacy}; its institutional component, the commercial, financial and managerial organisation of the economy, was destroyed and rebuilt twice from outside; and in 1913 all three were among the better-placed peripheral economies of the continent. The sections below take the three regimes in turn. \subsection{Interwar capitalism, 1913--1940} The First World War and the collapse of the empires gave Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia their first opportunity to build independent states, and left them in ruins. The German advance of 1915 stabilised along the Daugava, within reach of Riga, for two and a half years; the imperial government evacuated Latvia's industry eastwards, and most of it never returned; Riga lost more than half its population between 1914 and 1919 \parencites[107]{ehbaltics_tarvel}[616]{norkusmark2021}[103]{karnups_2017_neatkarigas}. Table~\ref{tab:war} places the result beside the other belligerents. Between 1913 and 1919 Latvia lost 35 per cent of its population, 59 per cent of its GDP and 37 per cent of its income per head, Lithuania 36, 60 and 38 per cent; of the European economies for which estimates exist, only the Soviet Union lost as large a share of its output. Estonia, untouched by major fighting until 1918, lost less. Pre-war Latvia had been called the `Belgium of the East' for its industry and living standards; by 1919 it resembled Belgium in the devastation it had suffered relative to its size \parencite[77]{hiden_salmon}. \input{../../Tables/latvia/T10_war.tex} The 1920s were a decade of reconstruction rather than growth. Lithuania regained its 1913 income per head by 1923, Estonia by 1925, Latvia only in \lvREGAINthirteen{}: the recovery was most protracted where the pre-war economy had been most integrated into the Russian market and most of the industrial capacity had been lost \parencites[95--6]{aldcroftthirdworld}[103]{eastern_crampton}[6]{norkus_2025_denmarkisation}. Between 1913 and 1929 income per head in the three countries together was unchanged (Table~\ref{tab:growth}), while the Western core grew by \grx{Western}{1913}{1929} per cent a year and Czechoslovakia, Berend's `success story of the twenties', by 45 per cent \parencite[243]{Berenddecadesofcrisis}; Latvia's 1922--9 growth of \gr{1922}{1929} per cent a year was bounce-back growth from a very low base, financed by foreign capital, and it stopped when the pre-war level was regained. The new states rebuilt on the land. Agrarian reforms expropriated the estates of the Baltic-German and Polish nobility, which had held between a quarter and a half of all land, and created a class of smallholders; gold-backed currencies were introduced in 1922 (Latvia and Lithuania) and 1928 (Estonia); exports were redirected from Russia to Britain and Germany and shifted from manufactures to butter, bacon, flax and timber, in conscious imitation of Denmark \parencites[115]{baltichistorykasekamp2017}{norkus_2025_denmarkisation}[121]{vaskela_1996_land}. Agriculture still employed 67 per cent of the Latvian labour force in the late 1930s and 63 and 74 per cent of the Estonian and Lithuanian (Table~\ref{tab:structure}). The 1930s look different. Between 1929 and 1938 income per head grew by \gr{1929}{1938} per cent a year in Latvia, \grx{Lithuania}{1929}{1938} in Lithuania and \grx{Estonia}{1929}{1938} in Estonia, against \grx{Western}{1929}{1938} per cent in the Western core, \grx{Periphery}{1929}{1938} in the Western periphery and \grx{ECE}{1929}{1938} in East-Central Europe; among European economies only the Soviet Union, whose figures for the period are contested, and Finland grew as fast, and all three Baltic states closed their gap with the Western core by six to ten percentage points (Table~\ref{tab:relative}).\footnote{Rosés and Wolf's Maddison-based estimates give Latvia 4.1 per cent a year over 1929--38 against 4.9 for the Soviet Union, and the authors note that the Latvian and Estonian figures may be on the high side \parencite[188, 190]{roseswolf2010}.} The Depression was shallower and shorter than in most of Europe: Lithuania avoided recession altogether, and Latvia's and Estonia's downturns of 1931--3, of 10 and 8 per cent from peak to trough, resembled those of the Nordic countries, which are regarded as among the mildest on the continent, although Latvia's banking crisis of 1931, in which three joint-stock banks failed, was more severe \parencites{grytten_nordicdepression}[91]{bernankegd01}[236]{terleckaspinigai}. The Baltic performance has usually been read, by contemporaries and by Aldcroft, as the fruit of export-led agricultural modernisation \parencites[189]{balticstates1938}[119--20]{aldcrof1914}. The sectoral evidence does not support that reading. Trade openness fell sharply after 1929, in Latvia from 38 to 22 per cent of GDP,\footnote{Period averages of 1925--9 and 1935--8 (Table~\ref{tab:structure}); the single-year ratios of Norkus and his co-authors, built on the same GDP series, fall from 49 per cent in 1929 to 27 in 1938 \parencite[10]{norkus_2025_why}.} the processed share of exports fell in both Latvia and Estonia, and the Baltic states remained the most agrarian and least industrial part of Europe outside the Balkans (Table~\ref{tab:structure}). What grew was industry for the home market: Latvian industrial output rose by \sgr{Industry}{1929}{1938} per cent a year over 1929--38, a rate exceeded among capitalist economies only by Lithuania and matched only by Finland, behind import-substituting tariffs, state enterprises and the infant-industry policies that the authoritarian governments of the 1930s, Lithuania's dating from 1926 and Estonia's and Latvia's from 1934, adopted as part of their `economic nationalism' \parencites[116]{ehbaltics_tarvel}{karnups_2017_karla}{Klimantas2024}. Latvia was the one Baltic economy in which the shares of both agriculture and industry in GDP rose in the 1930s at the expense of services, the result of heavily subsidised agriculture and the pruning of the public administration \parencites[683]{latvija19141945vesture}[135--6]{karnups_2017_karla}. The growth of the 1930s was achieved not through international trade but despite its contraction \parencite[188]{valge_1994_tartu}. \input{../../Tables/latvia/T9_structure.tex} The verdict on the interwar regime is mixed. Over 1913--38 as a whole, Latvian and Estonian income per head grew marginally faster than the Western core's, by \gr{1913}{1938} and \grx{Estonia}{1913}{1938} against \grx{Western}{1913}{1938} per cent a year, and Lithuanian marginally slower; the region's position relative to the core, \pctx{Baltics}{Western}{1913} per cent in 1913 and \pctx{Baltics}{Western}{1938} in 1938, did not change. The 1930s were among the most dynamic years the region has known, and by 1938 Latvia and Estonia retained the places among the best-performing peripheral economies of Europe that they had held in 1913, which is what Aldcroft meant in calling the Baltic states the most promising of Europe's backward regions \parencite[105, 171]{aldcroftthirdworld}. But the interwar years also disposed of a belief that has shaped Baltic self-perception ever since: that Latvia and Estonia stood level with Finland. The difference was not primarily one of social capability: Latvian literacy, though below Finnish (11 per cent of Latvians aged ten and over were illiterate in 1935, under 1 per cent of Finns aged fifteen and over in 1930), was high for the European periphery, and Latvian university enrolment per head, 4.3 per thousand in the 1930s, was nearly double the Western core's and, in Kalniņš's contemporary comparison, the highest in the Baltic \parencites{klimantas2025thesis}[102--3]{norkusdvides}. It was one of resources and markets. The losses were demographic before they were material: deportations, the Holocaust, war deaths and the flight of some 250,000 people to the West in 1944 removed more than a million people, among them a disproportionate share of the professional and commercial classes; the fall in income per head, 28 per cent in Latvia and 29 in Estonia, was correspondingly smaller than the fall in output, and roughly half the per-capita losses that Table~\ref{tab:war} records for Austria, the Netherlands or Poland. Lithuania's larger fall is examined in the companion paper. Recovery was rapid, as it was everywhere in the Soviet sphere: Latvia regained its 1938 level of total GDP in \sregain{GDP}, Estonia its 1939 level in 1948 and Lithuania in 1949, and with smaller populations their income per head regained the 1938 level in 1946, \lvREGAINthirtyeight{} and 1948 respectively, two years before the Western core or periphery regained theirs. The war had destroyed people rather than plant; with a fifth of the population of the northern republics gone, capacity stood underused, and the early recovery rested on putting labour, increasingly immigrant labour directed from Russia, back to work on existing capital, the mechanism that Vonyó and Markevich identify across post-war East-Central Europe \parencites[290]{vonyoinmorys2021}[108]{years_of_dependence}. The command economy was installed within five years. Industry and banks were nationalised in 1940--1 and again in 1945--7; the republics were incorporated into the all-Union planning system in 1946; and the deportations of 1948--53, which removed some 42,000 people from Latvia, 100,000 from Lithuania and 35,000 from Estonia, the largest single operation being that of March 1949, which took more than 40,000 people from Latvia and some 30,000 and 21,000 from Lithuania and Estonia, broke the resistance of the countryside to collectivisation, which was essentially complete within two years (Table~\ref{tab:collectivisation}) \parencites[183]{krumins_2017_tautsaimnieciba_1940}[99--100]{feest2014}[102--3]{years_of_dependence}. The agricultural indices record the cost. Latvian agricultural output, which had already fallen to 59 per cent of its 1938 level in 1947, hovered between 60 and 67 per cent through 1955, regained the pre-war level only in \sregain{Primary}, twenty-nine years after the pre-war peak, and never exceeded \primPEAKidx{} per cent of it before 1991, despite mechanisation and fertiliser; Estonia's recovery came in 1959 and Lithuania's in 1957.\footnote{Hiden and Salmon date Estonia's return to the 1938--9 level of agricultural output to the early 1960s, and Norkus and his co-authors put all three republics' return to 1938 levels in the early 1960s \parencites[131]{hiden_salmon}[15]{norkus_2025_denmarkisation}.} Nothing comparable to the Soviet famine of 1932--3 occurred, probably because the Baltic collectivisation did not coincide with a procurement crisis and because the system had by then learned to extract the surplus without destroying the herds; but in every Baltic republic the private plots that occupied a tenth of the land were producing a quarter to a third of agricultural output in 1989 \parencites{labsvirs_1959_case}[187--91]{years_of_dependence}. \input{../../Tables/latvia/T11_collectivisation.tex} What collectivisation did deliver was labour. Industry and construction expanded in the 1950s at rates the capitalist republics had never seen: Latvian industrial output grew by \sgr{Industry}{1950}{1968} per cent a year over 1950--68 and construction by \sgr{Construction}{1950}{1968}, Lithuanian industry by 10 per cent a year to 1975. The mechanism was the Soviet one of the 1930s, the forced migration of labour from countryside to town and the extraction of the agricultural surplus for reinvestment \parencite[99, 190, 211]{allenfarm}. Lithuania, where 80 per cent of the population still lived on the land in 1946, had the labour reserve to sustain it; Latvia and Estonia, more urban and with low fertility, did not, and the planners drew instead on immigration from the Russian interior, which raised Latvia's population by \lvPOPchangeSOVIET{} per cent between 1950 and 1989 and reduced ethnic Latvians to barely half of it \parencites[126--8]{baltichistorykasekamp2017}[42--4]{puur_2019_turbulent}[205]{grybkauskas_2011_sovietine}. Each republic was assigned a role in the Union's division of labour: Lithuania food processing, light industry and, later, oil refining and nuclear power; Estonia oil shale, electricity and textiles; Latvia machine-building, the electrotechnical and radio industry, railway rolling stock and microbuses, and a disproportionate share of all-Union and military enterprises \parencites[203--15]{years_of_dependence}{gatis_lv_eh}. Gerschenkron's late industrialiser borrows technology rather than inventing it and substitutes banks or the state for the prerequisites it lacks, and Solow's model predicts faster growth where capital per worker is scarce; Lewis's surplus labour raises average productivity as it moves off the land; and the cumulative effect of all three widens markets and permits scale economies \parencites[8]{gerschenkron1962}[70--1]{solow1956}{lewis1954}[22]{abramovitz_david1996}. But Abramovitz and David argued that the potential is realised only where the follower has the `social capability', the literacy, institutions, managerial competence and commercial organisation, to absorb what it borrows, and where the leader's technology is congruent with the follower's endowments; and Crafts and Toniolo, reading Europe's post-war golden age through that lens, found that even the apparently automatic catch-up of the 1950s and 1960s was conditioned on institutions and policies that fostered investment, technology transfer and the reallocation of resources \parencites[23--35]{abramovitz_david1996}[297--330]{craftstoniolo2010}. The Baltic states are an unusually clean test of these propositions. The human-capital component of their social capability, literacy and schooling, was high throughout, by the standards of the European periphery \parencite[71]{raun_2017_literacy}; its institutional component, the commercial, financial and managerial organisation of the economy, was destroyed and rebuilt twice from outside; and in 1913 all three were among the better-placed peripheral economies of the continent.
